messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-two when he first came to the clinic, though he moved with the careful deliberation of someone much older. A professional musician—he played classical guitar and had once performed at regional venues across California—he arrived for his intake appointment twenty minutes early, having circled the building twice to assess exits and sightlines. The stalking had begun three years ago, though its origins remained partly obscured to him even now. A woman he'd briefly dated, someone he'd met through a mutual friend at a concert, had become fixated on him. What had started as persistent texts and emails escalated into her showing up at venues where he performed, waiting outside his apartment, calling him at hours when she knew he'd be home. The police had issued a restraining order eighteen months in, but by then the damage to Marcus's sense of safety had already calcified.

He could not reconstruct the timeline of those early months with any clarity. There were gaps in what he remembered—entire weeks when she'd followed him to different neighborhoods, to coffee shops, to his ex-wife's house, and Marcus could only piece together these episodes from her own messages, from police reports, from the concerned calls of friends. The fragmentation terrified him because it meant she had been present in his life in ways he couldn't fully account for, couldn't fully remember. What haunted him most were the sudden, unbidden fragments that would surface without warning: the sound of her voice outside his door at three in the morning, the specific shade of her car in a parking lot, the feeling of being watched from across a crowded venue. These pieces would arrive with complete sensory force—he could smell the perfume she wore, could hear the exact cadence of her breathing—and then vanish as quickly as they'd come, leaving him disoriented and questioning what was real.

Marcus had come to believe he was weak, that a stronger man would have seen the danger earlier, would have handled it differently, would have been able to protect himself without needing police intervention. This conviction—that he was fundamentally inadequate—fed directly into his hypervigilance. He watched other people constantly now, scanning faces for signs of threat, interpreting neutral expressions as harbingers of malice. In his mind, if he had been stronger, more perceptive, less naive, he would not need to be this exhausted sentinel. The institutional failure compounded this self-judgment; the restraining order had felt like a bureaucratic gesture, a piece of paper that had not actually stopped her from finding him. The police had been sympathetic but ultimately powerless. The courts had failed him. This conviction that the systems meant to protect him were hollow made him feel more alone, more convinced that his own weakness was the only honest assessment of reality.

The memory gaps and those sudden sensory intrusions had become entangled with his threat assessment in ways that made him feel trapped. Because he couldn't remember when she'd been watching him, because fragments would arrive unbidden and vivid, he could never be certain when the danger had truly passed. Every unfamiliar place became a potential ambush; he avoided new restaurants, new routes to venues, anywhere he couldn't quickly map exits and sight lines. At night, the vigilance intensified. He felt safer during daylight, when he could see clearly and assess threats visually, but darkness made him feel hunted. He'd stopped accepting evening performance bookings. His income had declined. His ex-wife, concerned but ultimately exhausted by his withdrawal, had stopped calling as frequently.

The fragments still came—a flash of that specific perfume in a grocery store, a car that matched the color of hers turning a corner—and each one sent him spiraling back into the conviction that he was being watched, that his weakness had made him vulnerable, that no one could truly help him. He had come to the clinic because his last remaining regular gig, a Sunday morning teaching position at a community center, had become unsustainable; his hypervigilance was affecting his ability to teach, to trust even his students. What he most feared was that the vigilance was permanent, that he would never feel safe again, that the weakness he'd discovered in himself was not something that had been exposed by the stalking but something that defined him entirely.
